Substantial **reductions in inequality** have only ever been achieved as the **result of violent shocks**, primarily consisting of war, revolution, state failure and systems collapse, and plague.

According to Scheidel, the greatest **levelers** of the twentieth century did **not** include **peaceful social reforms**, they were the two world wars and the **communist revolutions**. More than **100 million people died** in each of the two world wars and in the communist social experiments.

Total War as a Great Leveler

World War II serves as Scheidel’s strongest example of “total war” leveling. Take Japan: In 1938, the wealthiest 1 percent of the population received 19.9 percent of all reported income before taxes and transfers. Within the next seven years, their share dropped by two-thirds, all the way down to 6.4 percent. More than half of this loss was incurred by the richest tenth of that top bracket: their income share collapsed from 9.2 percent to 1.9 percent in the same period, a decline by almost four-fifths. The declared real value of the income of the largest 1 percent of estates in Japan’s population fell by 90 percent between 1936 and 1945 and by almost 97 percent between 1936 to 1949. The top 0.1 percent of all estates lost even more during this period, 93 and 98 percent, respectively. During this period, the Japanese economic system was transformed as state intervention gradually created a planned economy that preserved only a facade of free-market capitalism. Executive bonuses were capped, rental income was fixed by the authorities, and between 1935 and 1943 the top income tax rate in Japan doubled.

Significant leveling also took place in other countries during wartime. According to Scheidel’s analysis, the two world wars were among the greatest levelers in history. The average percentage **drop of top income shares** in countries that actively fought in World War II as frontline states **was 31 percent** of the prewar level. This is a **robust finding** because the sample consists of a dozen countries. The only two countries in which inequality increased during this period were also those farthest from the major theaters of war (Argentina and South Africa).

Low savings rates and depressed asset prices, physical destruction and the loss of foreign assets, inflation and progressive taxation, rent and price controls, and nationalization all contributed in varying degrees to equalization. The wealth of the rich was dramatically reduced in the two world wars, whether countries lost or won, suffered occupation during or after the war, were democracies or run by autocratic regimes.

The **economic consequences** **of the** two **world wars were**, therefore, **devastating for the rich**—a fact that stands in direct **opposition to the thesis** that it was **capitalists** that **instigated the wars** **in pursuit of** their own **economic interests.** Contrary to the popular perception that the lower classes suffered most in the wars, in economic terms it was the capitalists who were the biggest losers.

Incidentally, the left-wing economist Thomas Piketty comes to a similar conclusion. In his book Capital in the Twenty-First Century, he argues that progressive taxation in the twentieth century was primarily a product of the two world wars and not of democracy.

Poverty is Eliminated Peacefully

The price of reducing inequality has thus usually involved violent shocks and catastrophes, whose v**ictims have been** not only the rich but millions and **millions of people**. Neither nonviolent land reforms nor economic crises nor democratization has had as great a leveling effect throughout recorded history as these violent upheavals. If the goal is to distribute income and wealth more equally, says historian Scheidel, then we simply cannot close our eyes to the violent ruptures that have so often proved necessary to achieve that goal. We must ask ourselves whether humanity has ever  succeeded in equalizing the distribution of wealth without considerable violence. Analyzing thousands of years of human history, Scheidel’s answer is no. This may be a depressing finding for many adherents of egalitarian ideas.

However, if we shift perspective, and ask not “How do we reduce inequality?” but “**How do we reduce poverty?**” then we can provide an optimistic answer: Not violent ruptures of the kind that led to reductions of inequality, but very **peaceful mechanisms**, namely **innovations and growth**, brought about **by the forces of capitalism**, have **led to** the **greatest declines in poverty**. Or, to put it another way: The greatest “levelers” in history have been violent events such as wars, revolutions, state and systems collapses, and pandemics, but the greatest poverty reducer in history has been capitalism. **Before capitalism** came into being, **most of the world**’s population **was living in extreme poverty**—in 1820, the rate stood at **90 percent. Today,** it’s **down to** less than **10 percent**. And the most remarkable aspect of all this progress is that, in the recent decades since the **end of communism in China** and other countries, the **decline in poverty has accelerated to a pace unmatched** in any previous period of human history. In 1981, the rate was still 42.7 percent; by 2000, it had fallen to 27.8 percent, and in 2021 it was only 9.3 percent.

## Other Answers 

### AT: Biopolitics 

#### All of this is nothing. 

**Birch 17**, \[Kean Birch, Ontario Research Chair in Science Policy and Professor in the Department of Science, Technology, and Society and the Graduate Program in Science & Technology Studies at York University, Canada, Director of the Institute for Technoscience & Society with a specialization in assetization, 09-22-2017, "The problem of bio-concepts: biopolitics, bio-economy and the political economy of nothing," ADS, https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017CSSE...12..915B/abstract, accessed 07-09-2026\] // oast

In previous work, David Tyfield and I argue that these bio-concepts represent a problematic attempt in STS discussions to theorize contemporary capitalism without actually theorizing contemporary capitalism (Birch and Tyfield 2013). We mean that the fetishization of the biological – e.g. bioscience, biotechnology – is not an adequate basis for understanding the transformation of political-economic knowledges, practices and processes over the last few decades, let alone century or so. These changes are frequently ignored or sidelined in the STS literature. It is noticeable, for example, that very few STS scholars theorizing the bio-economy actually engage (rigorously) with literature from political economy, heterodox economics or orthodox economics, even just to treat them as an object of study. This gap in their theoretical approach belies the general tenor of their claims (e.g. capitalism has been transformed by biotechnology). In contrast, it is my contention that any theorizing of the bio-economy necessarily means that we must examine how political-economic actors understand, practice and reconfigure their political economies. This means going beyond the biosciences and actually delving into issues of economic belief, accounting, corporate governance, finance and so on. **Doing this, however, reveals a stark reality about all these bio- concepts; they may actually be theorizing nothing at all. The evidence used to support these bio-concepts is often limited at best,** especially in light of the general – or, dare I say, grand – claims being made. Again, I am focusing on the discussion of the bio- economy, rather than biopolitics more broadly. What I want to highlight is three areas where bio-concepts are used to make very broad claims, and yet where evidence is limited or contradictory. These areas are: (1) clinical labour, (2) bio-citizenship, and (3) bio-economy.

First, a key part of Cooper and Waldby's (2014) argument is that new forms of embodied labour, like surrogacy and tissue donation, are significant phenomena worthy of our attention. While there is no doubt that these are important issues for those involved, they are not quantitatively significant. Cooper and Waldby (2014: 230, fn6) claim that there were 17,697 egg donations in 2009 in the USA. That means the proportion of donor births in the USA in 2009 was 0.43% - there were 4.13 million births in 2009 (Martin et al. 2011). A proportion below 1% does not support the notion of a general trend as suggested by the theorizing of 'clinical labour' and the claim that “these markets are vast” (p.9). Similarly, the percentage of donations in European countries is very low (p.69). Now, clinical labour involves more than egg donation, it also involves surrogacy and clinical trial participation. As Cooper and Waldby acknowledge, there are limited data on surrogacy in their case of India, “so it is impossible to estimate precise scale, and our account is necessarily impressionistic” (pp.78-9). What they further suggest is that the surrogacy business was worth $445 million in 2008, although it is not clear for whom. This, again, is hardly a significant number, however. It is only with clinical trials that there are a significant number of people involved, upwards of 1.7 million people in the USA (p.230, fn6). What this implies is that clinical labour is of limited theoretical relevance beyond clinical trial participation. Considering this is probably one of the few ways that citizens directly interact with technoscience once they finish their education, it is perhaps pertinent for a discipline like science education to engage with this area directly (see Weinstein 2008).

Second, another popular bio-concept is the notion of bio-citizenship evidenced in the increasing engagement publics have with modern biotechnologies (e.g. Rose and Novas 2004). This is especially linked to the role played by patient advocacy groups in setting research priorities, providing funding, etc. (Rose 2001). While there is no doubt that patient advocacy groups are increasingly important social actors, this does not mean that the idea of bio-citizenship can be generalized to broader publics. It is important to remember that most people have no idea about the ins and outs of genetics, genomics, synthetic biology, etc., beyond what they pick up from newspapers, magazines, television, internet, etc. In this context, it is difficult to understand how people can become self-governing, biological citizens when – in the European context, at least – they have never even heard of things like synthetic biology (83%), biobanks (67%), or nanotechnology (55%) (Gaskell et al. 2010). Even where publics have heard of something, it is not self-evident that they understand biotechnologies in a technoscientific sense, which then problematizes the notion that the biosciences are leading to the increasing ‘genomic’ self-governing of our identities, subjectivities and citizenship. It is more apt to suggest that these things are being reshaped by the intermediaries of science and publics, which would have important implications for science education. Again, it would suggest the need to engage citizens in continuous forms of learning about technoscience, which necessitates the expansion of non-formal education sites, formats, fora, etc. It also means challenging the role of intermediaries in science education (e.g. media, business, education institutes, etc.), examining how they imagine and frame publics in order to problematize claims about ‘proper’ public understandings of science (Landström et al. forthcoming). Finally, when it comes to the conceptualization of the bio-economy there is a real need to be more moderate in the claims made about it. While people like Waldby (2000), Rose (2001), Sunder Rajan (2006) and Cooper (2008) emphasize the transformational implication of biotechnologies on the economy and society, others have highlighted a much less dramatic impact, if any at all. To start, a range of research demonstrates that the notion of a 'biotechnology revolution' is somewhat overblown. Research by Nightingale and Martin (2004), for example, shows that there is a significant mismatch between expectations and outcomes in the bio-economy. While Sunder Rajan and Cooper both highlight the role of promises and expectations in their analyses, they tend to fall into the trap of buying into the hype (Taussig 2010). In contrast, research by Hopkins et al. (2007) shows that it is precisely because it is not revolutionary that biotechnology is so hyped. What is interesting about all this is that the underwhelming performance of the bio-economy stretches back to the late 1970s and is evident in the poor performance of public biotechnology companies (Pisano 2006). That means it is not a sudden reversal of previous excellence. This poor performance is evident across a number of variables (Ernst and Young 2012; Huggett and Lähteenmäki 2012):

• Profit: the global biotechnology industry was not profitable from its inception in 1976 until 2007; global profits were US$6.8 billion in 2011.

• Equity performance: publicly-listed, global biotechnology companies performed reasonably well when it came to revenues as proportion of market capitalization before 2007 (ranging between a ratio of 6-7 to 1); however, after 2007, and when they became profitable for the first time, they performance on this measure fell significantly (ratio of 4-4.5 to 1).

• Products: only a few, usually large, biopharmaceutical companies have ever managed to launch a product; most other companies are bought out before this happens.

What is evident from the quantitative data is that the global bio-economy – at least in the biomedical sector – is represented by about 15 companies (out of over 4000), which represent a majority of revenues, profits, market capitalization, and product sales. What is most significant about this is that market capitalization (US$403 billion in 2011) dwarfs any revenues from product sales or trade in biological tissue highlighted by STS scholars (e.g. Cooper and Waldby 2014). It is not, therefore, that STS scholars are necessarily incorrect to examine the importance of the bio-economy; it is that their focus on bio-concepts has blinded them to other, more important issues that are not bound up with biological materiality. Again, science education is important here. It would seem important, for example, to examine technoscience from a diversity of angles in order to understand its relevance to and impact on our lives; this means engaging critically with the political, social and economic implications of science and innovation. More specifically, it means challenging the very notion that science and innovation are unalloyed public goods that should be left alone by unruly publics who do not know any better (Wynne and Welsh 2013). Science education offers a way to engage publics to pursue greater oversight of technoscience at a time when they otherwise risk being turned into compliant consumers (Thorpe and Gregory 2010).

Conclusion

While there has undoubtedly been a transformation in the way that the state, economy and society are configured, whether this can be directly attributed to new biosciences and biotechnologies is debatable. My intention in this article was to question the way that many STS scholars have sought to relate modern bioscience to modern capitalism in the emergence of the (so-called) bio-economy. As such I sought to examine a number of popular bio-concepts, especially those building on the work of Michel Foucault in his work on biopolitics. In so doing I have criticized a number of these bio- concepts and how they are deployed in research on biotechnology. My main foil in this analysis was the work of Cooper and Waldby (2014) on clinical labour, although I also sought to ensure that my comments reflect wider concerns with the STS literature. I then finished by discussing how these bio-concepts often lack empirical support for their generic claims, although that is not to say that they have nothing to say when it comes to specific cases they address. **What I think is missing in many of these bio-concepts is the necessary nuance to acknowledge that the theoretical insights they provide are often limited, context-dependent and particular to the case in hand. They are not generalizable to wider society, economy and polity. This does not mean they are not useful, it just means that they cannot represent a grand new understanding of the world.**
